connections.observation: χρεία recurs throughout as the generating and structuring principle of the city (s001), yet when the city is declared potentially complete (s015), justice and injustice are asked to be located ποῦ ἐν αὐτῇ, and Adeimantus tentatively answers εἰ μή που ἐν αὐτῶν τούτων χρείᾳ τινὶ τῇ πρὸς ἀλλήλους (s016). The conjunction makes visible that the very force said to create the city—need in relation to one another—is now proposed as the possible site where justice might be found within it.

The reciprocal ἄλλος ἄλλον/ἄλλῳ construction (s003) articulates differentiated persons taking and giving in relation to one another; μεταδίδωσι/μεταλαμβάνει (s009) names the action of sharing and receiving between them. Held together, the two configurations make visible that reciprocal exchange is enacted through grammatically paired persons and verbs of transmission, and this same reciprocal structure returns at 371b when the question πῶς ἀλλήλοις μεταδώσουσιν is posed—the formula by which the city was founded becomes the question the city must now answer internally.

The individual is declared οὐκ αὐτάρκης (s006), generating the city; later, the διάκονος goes and returns κενός (s011) unless the city produces surplus. The conjunction reveals a doubled insufficiency: the person lacks and founds the city; the city's agent goes empty unless the city exceeds its own needs—sufficiency remains elusive at both scales.

The formula εἷς ἓν κατὰ φύσιν (s008) resolves the question of specialization; σχολή (s022) appears first as what the work will not wait for, then as what the specialized worker enjoys—leisure from other tasks. Together they make visible that specialization according to nature produces not only better work but a temporal condition: the worker gains σχολή from other things precisely by attending to the one thing that will not wait.

The three primary needs are enumerated in ordinal sequence—πρώτη (food), δευτέρα (shelter), τρίτη (clothing) (s004)—as abstract categories; later, a dense cluster of concrete material goods appears (s017): σῖτος, οἶνος, ἱμάτια, ὑποδήματα, κριθαί, πυροί, μάζαι, ἄρτοι. The conjunction makes visible that the abstract ranking of needs is answered by a material abundance that exceeds the schema—wine is added to grain, barley and wheat are distinguished, both maza and bread appear—the simple city's life overflows its founding enumeration.

κοινωνία is invoked at the city's founding as partners and helpers (s007), returns in the question of whether to share labor, and is named as the city's purpose (κοινωνίαν ποιησάμενοι πόλιν ᾠκίσαμεν); yet the μισθωτοί are defined as τὰ μὲν τῆς διανοίας μὴ πάνυ ἀξιοκοινώνητοι (s013)—unfit for intellectual partnership. The conjunction makes visible that the very city founded on κοινωνία includes a class declared ἀξιοκοινώνητοι in mind, participating only by selling bodily strength.

ἔμποροι and κάπηλοι are distinguished spatially—πλανήτας versus ἱδρυμένους (s012)—and named alongside μισθωτοί as distinct exchange roles (s010); all are repeatedly called διάκονοι (s023). Held together, the configuration makes visible that the expanding city generates a series of intermediary figures differentiated by motion (wandering/settled), location (agora/between cities), and commodity (goods/bodily labor), yet all are comprehended under διακονία—service that mediates between producers and needs.

The city is made in speech τῷ λόγῳ ἐξ ἀρχῆς and asked whether it has grown τελέα (s015); it closes with two negative restraints: not begetting beyond means, guarding against πενία and πόλεμον (s020). The conjunction reveals that the completion of the city is immediately followed not by achieved sufficiency but by cautions—poverty and war are named as threats at the very moment the city is declared potentially whole, and πόλεμος appears for the first time in the section precisely here.

Summer and winter are contrasted through paired participles—naked/unshod versus clothed/shod (s018)—meeting the earlier enumerated need for ἐσθής and ὑποδήματα; but the description continues into reclining on beds of smilax and myrtle, feasting, drinking wine, garlanded, hymning the gods (s019). Together they make visible that seasonal necessity is satisfied, then exceeded: the simple city's life includes ritual festivity and divine address beyond the needs that generated it.

The οἰκ- root threads through dwelling, co-dwelling, building, settling, founding (s021); the four craftsmen (s005) correspond to the primary needs, with the οἰκοδόμος directly answering οἴκησις. The conjunction makes visible that building/dwelling vocabulary saturates the entire founding sequence—the city is named a συνοικία, shelter is the second need, the builder is the second craftsman, and the question of κατοικίσαι the city in a place that needs no imports arises—yet that proves ἀδύνατον, and the simple citizens end by οἰκοδομησάμενοι οἰκίας in actuality. The vocabulary of dwelling moves from the city's name through its structure to the concrete act of house-building.

παρασκευή recurs from the question of how the city will supply needs through to citizens described as παρεσκευασμένοι (s014); forms of δέομαι/δεῖ recur throughout from founding neediness through expanding requirements (s002). Held together, they make visible that the section's movement is simultaneously a movement of provision and a movement of need—as the city παρασκευάζει more, it also δεῖται more—the two vocabularies rise together rather than the first resolving the second.

χρεία generates the city, ranks needs, drives trade, and is proposed as justice's possible locus (s001); the agora, coinage as σύμβολον, and silver arise together as institutions of exchange (s024). The conjunction reveals that need, having founded the city through direct reciprocal sharing (μεταδίδωσι ἄλλος ἄλλῳ), generates new mediating institutions—the marketplace and money as σύμβολον τῆς ἀλλαγῆς—need produces not only persons and roles but symbolic systems of equivalence.

new_signals.observation: ἦ γάρ; recurs four times as Socrates' confirmatory question after articulating a step in the city's construction or a definition, punctuating the building sequence.
πάνυ μὲν οὖν recurs eight times as Adeimantus's characteristic assent, creating a rhythmic pattern of proposal and agreement structuring the entire city-building.

elements.form: τέτταρτον μέρος... ἐν τετάρτῳ μέρει... τὰ δὲ τρία
elements.context: The farmer's time divided into fourths

new_signals.observation: The question of whether the farmer should share with four others or work for himself alone is articulated through precise numerical division: one-fourth of the food in one-fourth of the time, the other three-fourths distributed among house, clothing, shoes—the alternative to κοινωνία is calculated partition.

elements.context: Paired negative constructions in the farmer question

new_signals.observation: The negative conjunction καὶ μή appears twice in immediate succession as the farmer's self-sufficient alternative is articulated—first μὴ ἄλλοις κοινωνοῦντα πράγματα ἔχειν, then ἀλλʼ αὐτὸν διʼ αὑτὸν—the formula marks withdrawal from κοινωνία.

elements.context: τῷ λόγῳ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ποιῶμεν πόλιν
ποιήσει δὲ αὐτήν... ἡ ἡμετέρα χρεία
οὐχ ὑπὲρ τὴν οὐσίαν ποιούμενοι τοὺς παῖδας

new_signals.observation: ποιέω recurs throughout the city's construction—first as the deliberate making in speech, then as what need will do, then as the work of each craftsman, then as domestic production, finally as begetting children—the verb threads through founding, crafting, producing, and reproducing.

elements.form: τίνʼ οἴει ἀρχὴν ἄλλην πόλιν οἰκίζειν;
elements.context: Socrates' question about the city's beginning

elements.form: τῷ λόγῳ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ποιῶμεν πόλιν
elements.context: Proposal to make the city from the beginning in speech

new_signals.observation: ἀρχή appears twice in immediate succession: first as the ἀρχή (principle/beginning) that founds any city, answered as human non-self-sufficiency; then as the ἐξ ἀρχῆς (from the beginning) of making a city in speech—the founding principle becomes the starting point of deliberate construction.
